Yes. The story mostly unfolds close to real time, which suits a single short ferry crossing. It compresses only where useful: the decades Ilse has run the ferry and the old man's childhood with two ferries each get a line or two, conveying history without slowing the scene.

The phone call is gently stretched. The vibration stops, restarts, the passengers react, Ilse grips the rudder, and the message flashes on the display. This lingers on the one moment of inner tension without overdoing it. The approach to the far bank is then compressed with "Nach einer Weile," releasing the tension at the right pace. The rhythm feels deliberate and matches the quiet, foggy mood.
